c.v: The Test Bench logs wheel encoder readings as text, one per line:
. Write the C++ declaration of a function that parses one line. Then write its preconditions, its postconditions, and what it does for each way a line can be wrong. Take 10 minutes.

The central point is that there is no precondition on the text. A line comes from a file, so no caller can promise that it is well formed, and everything that can be wrong with it belongs in the error contract: too few or too many fields, a field that isn't a number, a number that doesn't fit in 64 bits, a negative time stamp. Negative ticks are fine, because the robot can reverse. The result type says that the caller gets either a sample or a reason, and
stops a caller from dropping both.

You pass if your function takes a view of the text, reports at least three kinds of error as a value rather than a sentinel such as -1, and states what the fields hold on success. Treating malformed text as a precondition, or leaving out the postcondition, is a partial pass. No error contract at all is a fail.

A contract states what each side of an interface promises, in four parts. A precondition is what the caller must make true before the call. A postcondition is what the function makes true on a normal return. An invariant is what stays true of an object between calls to its public members, established by the constructor and kept after. An error contract says what the function does when it can't meet its postcondition: which errors, reported how, what state is left behind. Types are the part a compiler checks; the rest lives in comments, checks, or, from C++26, the language itself.

The problem this solves is a promise nobody wrote down. Three plain doubles in a row say nothing about which is which or what unit each is in, so a caller can swap two wheels or pass millimetres for metres, and the compiler says nothing. Input from outside the process, a file, a message, the network, is never a precondition: no caller can guarantee it arrived well formed, and treating it as one turns an operator mistake into a crash instead of a reported error.

The mechanism is telling a broken precondition apart from an error, then pushing as much of the rest into the type system as it will hold. A broken precondition is a bug in the caller, fixed in code and stopped loudly, close to where it happened; an error is an outcome the caller expects and has to handle. A named struct of wheel ticks, or a position tagged with its frame, makes a class of mistake fail to compile; a message crossing a process boundary can't carry that, so the check moves to run time against a fixed definition.

What it costs is a choice of three ways to report an error, each losable differently. An error code is dropped silently unless its type is marked so ignoring it won't compile. An exception can't be ignored, but one left uncaught ends the process, taking a whole ROS node down with it. A result type still fails if the caller reads the wrong alternative unchecked.

You meet this in the interview question itself: write the preconditions, postconditions and errors for a function parsing one line of a file, where the answer that matters is that it has no precondition on the text at all, because everything wrong with it belongs in the error contract instead.

c.v: The line between a precondition and an error matters more than the names. A broken precondition is a bug in the caller. The fix is in the code, and the right response is to stop loudly, as close to the bug as possible. An error is an outcome the caller expects and has to handle: a missing file, a line that doesn't parse, a full disk. Input from outside the process, such as files, messages, the network or a person, is never a precondition, because no caller can guarantee it. A parser has no precondition on its text, and everything wrong with the text goes into its error contract.

A contract also has to survive change. Once another team, a log file or a recorded bag depends on a message, its definition is fixed: adding a field, renaming one or changing its type changes the bytes on the wire, while the type name stays the same. Since Iron, each ROS 2 interface carries a hash of its definition, and

, and publish both until every consumer has moved. A file format carries a version number in its header, and a reader refuses a major version it doesn't know instead of guessing.

A contract is tested clause by clause. Each error in the error contract gets a test that provokes it and checks both the error and the state left behind. A postcondition gets a test over many inputs, often a round trip: write a value, parse it back, compare. An invariant gets a test that tries to break it through the public members. A precondition check gets at most a test that it fires, such as GoogleTest's

, because a program in which it fires is already wrong. At a message boundary, the consumer's tests replay messages the producer really sent, such as a recorded bag, so a change on either side fails a test before it reaches the robot.

items.v: The reader's postcondition says how long its result lives: the view borrows the reader's buffer until the next call. That is a borrowing contract, and the next topic follows such borrows through a pipeline. Returning a
would remove the rule at the price of a copy per line. The end of the input is not an error, so it is an empty

The truncated last line never reaches the processor. The parser reports it as
skips and counts it, which is the right choice for a log whose last line a crash can cut.

The processor's invariant is visible in the output. The sample at 1.15 s is refused, and the motion at 1.3 s is computed from the sample at 1.2 s, as if the refused one had never arrived. The wheel sizes come from configuration, which is input from outside, so they are checked in the constructor, which throws when it can't establish the invariant (
). An odometer with a zero wheel base can do nothing useful, so the run doesn't start.
The writer throws when a write fails, which is Core Guidelines
: throw when a function can't do the job it was given. Skipping the line and carrying on would leave an output file that looks complete and isn't.
counts everything that was skipped. A silent skip hides a sensor that sends garbage for an hour, and a count makes it visible to the operator and to tests.
